Auction Report, Market Trends

14 Eye-Catching Cars From the 2026 Broad Arrow Audrain Auction

Rick Carey
08 October 2026
Share

Stay up to speed with stories written by drivers, for drivers.

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by

This sale marked Broad Arrow’s first sale at Audrain Motor Week in Newport, Rhode Island. It was also Broad Arrow’s first auction anywhere in the Northeast, although its specialists have abundant experience in the region. The consignment, let it be said, was diverse with many categories not usually represented in the region’s few catalog sales. It felt like a wide-ranging sampling of the Audrain/New England market to see what appealed to local collectors, and persuaded them to loosen up their famously tight Yankee purse strings.

Notably absent were contemporary seven-figure supercars, with only a Ferrari 430 Scuderia and Mercedes-Benz AMG SLS impinging upon the lower end of that value stratosphere. Given that absence, overall sale totals amounted to $8.3M, with a handsome sale percentage of 87.7% bolstered by 48 No Reserve cars (of the 65 lots offered). Eight of the 17 remaining lots reached their reserves, a 47% sell-through rate on reserved consignments. 

For some who may be tired of all the attention that Ferraris, Paganis, Bugattis and the like are getting atop recent auction results lists, be heartened by Broad Arrow’s top sale at Audrain: A 1914 Stutz Bearcat. It was a hit at $1,875,000 all-in, even though it previously sold in 2021’s feverish market for $2,920,000. The other two seven-figure cars were 300SLs, a Gullwing and a Roadster, that didn’t meet reserve. 

Well attended during the auction if a little sparse at the preview, Broad Arrow acquitted itself well in its Audrain consignment, presentation and conduct, and provided a sound basis for next year’s reprise. 

Lot 112: 1972 Toyota Land Cruiser FJ43

Chassis no. FJ4324324; Engine no. F377783. Rustic Green with ivory vinyl top over gray vinyl. Recent restoration, #2+ condition.

Equipment: 3878-cc/155-hp six-cylinder, four-speed, AVM locking front hubs, BF Goodrich tires, center-facing rear seats, rear-mounted spare.

Condition: Restored like new and driven 1595km (991 miles) since, but still looking pristine and with better-than-new cosmetics. A thoroughly and professionally restored FJ43.

Bottom line: Reportedly sold new in Colombia, and restored by FJ specialists there about 10 years ago. There seems to be an endless supply of Land Cruisers in Central and South America, and the soft-top FJ43 is a model not sold in the U.S., so there is a pipeline bringing them in for hungry American buyers at a premium price over what they sell for south of the border. The $70,000–$90,000 estimate here emphasizes the “wow” factor, but the bidders paid only for its quality and practicality.  

Lot 128: 1970 Dodge Coronet R/T Hemi 2-Door Hardtop

Sold for $207,200

Chassis no. WS23R0G219666. Plum Crazy Purple over white vinyl. Older restoration, #2 condition.

Equipment: 426-cid/425-hp Hemi V-8, four-speed, Hurst pistol-grip shifter, Rally wheels with trim rings, Goodyear Polyglas GT tires, eight-track stereo, Ramcharger air intake.

Condition: Restored like new and kept that way. Excellent cosmetics. Represented as matching numbers, and broadcast sheet documented.

Bottom line: Sold at Barrett-Jackson in 2003 for $170,640, then at RM Monterey in 2008 for $156,750. This strong result is confirming evidence that the Hemi’s allure is still as strong as the engine itself. Equally alluring is the Plum Crazy paint and, at least to a driver, the four-speed. It is a strong car, and it brought strong money.  

Lot 139: 1933 Rover 14/6 Speed Pilot Sports Tourer by Carbodies

Sold for $42,000

Chassis no. 36173. Light gray with gray fenders and black cloth top over dark gray leather. Recent restoration, #2 condition.

Equipment: RHD. 1577-cc/47-hp six-cylinder, four-speed, body-color wire wheels, Goodrich tires, folding windshield, Lucas headlights.

Condition: Excellent paint, bright chrome, and lightly used upholstery. Bright, crisp gauges. Done and maintained to very high standards. Believed to be the only four-door Sports Tourer built on this chassis and one of very few 14/6s (aka “Speed Pilot” or “Speed Fourteen”) of any type to still survive.

Bottom line: Sold by Broad Arrow at Amelia in 2024 for $67,200 and a relative bargain here whether compared with the 2024 sale or this auction’s $50,000–$70,000 pre-sale estimate. This is an attractive and sporting-looking if somewhat obscure British tourer with a (small) six-cylinder engine bought for (prewar) MG Midget money.  

Lot 114: 1965 Alfa Romeo Giulia Sprint GT Coupe Restomod

Sold for $56,000

Chassis no. AR614896. Red with yellow nose highlight over gray leatherette. Modified restoration, #3+ condition.

Equipment: Modified 2-liter “Twin Spark” engine, five-speed, limited-slip differential, Koni shocks, Pittatore cams, 14″ alloy wheels, Falken tires, Prototipo leather-wrapped steering wheel, Spanish Weber carburetors, stainless exhaust, Alfaholics alloy fuel tank.

Condition: Upgraded in the 2010s. Chipguarded nose. No bumpers. Very good paint and interior. Clean but original underbody. Orderly, clean, and tidy engine compartment. A very pretty and potentially exciting driver with excellent cosmetics, ideal for AONE’s upcoming Cape Cod Tour.

Bottom line: As a restomod, this is a “name your price” car. It almost certainly cost more to build than the $90,000 low estimate. Inviting to look at and reassuring in its mechanical presentation, it begs to be driven home. And at this price, it will be driven home as a solid value that could have brought even more.  

Lot 106: 1924 Studebaker Big Six Seven-Passenger Sedan by Fisher

Sold for $36,400

Chassis no. 20031367; Engine no. EK32770. Maroon with black roof and fenders over brown cloth. Cosmetic restoration, #3- condition.

Equipment: 354-cid/60-hp six-cylinder, three-speed, tinted glass visor, disc wheels, dual sidemounts, Motometer, Bausch and Lomb headlights, jump seats, luggage trunk, wood steering wheel, Waltham dash clock, rear window shade.

Condition: Tired and superficial Harrah’s restoration. Moth-eaten upholstery. Dull paint. Worn and chipped. Dirty, mostly original chassis. Although this car was described as a Harrah’s Gold Star restoration, it doesn’t appear to have ever been done to that standard and has not aged well.

Bottom line: Bought four months ago at Bonhams’ auction of National Automobile Museum collection cars for $21,280. The owner enjoyed a tidy return even at this result, which hammered sold for well under the (optimistic) low estimate of $45K. The result is a reasonable compromise, and bought a car with potential and ample performance.  

Lot 113: 1970 Ferrari 246 Dino GT

Sold for $456,000

Chassis no. 00908; Engine no. 005748. Giallo Fly over Navy Blue. Recent restoration, #2+ condition.

Equipment: 2419-cc/195-hp V-6, five-speed, Dino badges, Cromodora centerlock alloy wheels, Michelin XWX tires, tool roll, jack, trophies.

Condition: Concours-quality restoration, clean and essentially unused. Multiple Platinum award winner at Cavallino and FCA events. Done right without being overdone.

Bottom line: Sold by RM at Monterey a year ago for $434,000 and brought about 5% more today, a strong result helped by the dramatic colors, impressive condition, and its position as the most appealing Ferrari in this auction.  

Lot 123: 1937 Packard 1501 Super Eight Convertible Victoria

Sold for $123,200

Chassis no. 1007279; Engine no. 400285A. Packard Cream with brown cloth top over saddle leather. Older restoration, #2+ condition.

Equipment: 320-cid/135-hp straight-eight, three-speed, heater, radio, steel wheels, wide whitewalls, dual enclosed sidemounts with mirrors.

Condition: Excellent paint, chrome, interior, and top. Attractive woodgrain but scratched steering wheel finish. A cleanly restored, nearly pristine chassis. Ready to show. The restoration is a quarter century old but could have been done last year from its appearance.

Bottom line: This is a particularly impressive Packard, clothed in an attractive body style. It impressed at every level and attracted a stream of admirers during the preview, even some much too young to have gained an appreciation for classic-era Packards when growing up. The result is a reasonable compromise between history and quality and represents a good value, as the truly great classic cars last longer than their natural audience.

Lot 148: 1957 Oldsmobile Starfire 98 Convertible

Sold for $44,800

Chassis no. 579L04098. Jade Mist with white accent and white vinyl top over green leather. Older restoration, #2- condition.

Equipment: 371-cid/300-hp V-8 with J-2 triple carburetors, automatic, spinner wheel covers, whitewalls, power antenna and windows, air conditioning, power steering and brakes, power seat, Autronic Eye, WonderBar radio, driving lights.

Condition: Very good paint. Sound original upholstery showing age and use. Tight-fitting top. Restored underbody and chassis with stone-chipped front wheel wells. Mismatched headlights. A 2005 AACA NFP restoration, now aged and driven but still impressive. The J-2 carbs are a nice bonus.

Bottom line: This is a huge value, at least 50% less than what would be reasonably expected given the car’s extensive list of equipment and accessories and its generally very good cosmetics. There appeared to be no tangible reason other than the restoration’s age to discount it. The buyer got a no-reserve, everyone-had-gone-to-the-bathroom, price. Great buy.

Lot 117: 2009 Ferrari F430 Scuderia Coupe

Sold for $538,500

Chassis no. ZFFKW64A0167230. Bianco Avus with silver stripes over Tessuto cloth and Alcantara. Original, #2- condition.

Equipment: 4308-cc/503-hp, six-speed F1 gearbox, matte gray 19″ wheels, Pirelli P Zero tires, Scuderia shields, carbon-ceramic brakes, black calipers, CD changer. Assembly no. 84584.

Condition: Represented with 25,454 miles but looks barely used, and represented to have had a major service in 2025 and September 2026.

Bottom line: Lighter, stronger, track-tuned, performance-focused, and rare compared to the standard F430, the Scuderia has been a market darling this year, with rapidly rising prices for well-kept examples like this. It’s way more expensive than it might have been a year ago but probably not as expensive as it’s going to be next year, though it’s less than what other, lower-mile Scuderias have sold for in recent months.  

Lot 124: 1956 Continental Mk II

Sold for $173,600

Chassis no. C56E2881. Deep Green over green leather. Older restoration, #2- condition.

Equipment: 368-cid/285-hp V-8, automatic, Town & Country radio, wheel covers, Coker wide whitewall tires, power windows.

Condition: Excellent paint in a gorgeous and effective color. Air conditioning installed during restoration. A lovely example of a lovely car. Two-time Owners’ Club winner in 2003 and 2009. Still nearly impeccable.

Bottom line: The paint color was particularly notable, a subtle dark metallic green that highlighted the Mark II’s beautiful lines. It drew plenty of attention and a realistic price even though it came in over the $125,000 high estimate. There aren’t many Mark IIs that are this pretty and impressively maintained.  

Lot 164: 1970 Alfa Romeo Giulia Super Berlina

Sold for $39,200

Chassis no. AR1876178. Blu Olandese over tan vinyl. Visually maintained, largely original, #3 condition.

Equipment: 1570-cc/98-hp four-cylinder, Weber carburetors, five-speed, 15″ Campagnolo alloy wheels, Yokohama tires, multiband radio, halogen headlights and fog lights, lowered, tools, jack.

Condition: An Italian market car, imported to the U.S. in 2018, then repainted, and bought by the consignor in 2022. Decent repaint and reupholstered front seats, but an old back seat with tears. Euro gauges. Chintzy floor mats. A presentable driver.

Bottom line: Presentable it may be, but it’s also rare and will make a wonderful tour and weekend car. It is well turned out and gives some confidence in the way it has been prepared, redone, and maintained. The result is right on the money and splits the difference in the pre-sale estimate of $30,000–$40,000.  

Lot 159: 1932 Ford Hot Rod High Boy Roadster

Sold for $42,000

Chassis no. 0513990066. Candy Apple Red over white vinyl. Modified restoration, #2+ condition.

Equipment: 347-cid Ford V-8, Top-loader four-speed, four-barrel, Edelbrock polished intake manifold, heater, body-color steel wheels, hubcaps and trim rings, whitewalls, chrome suspension, Ford 9″ rear, limited-slip, Stewart Warner gauges, transverse leaf springs, top, side curtains.

Condition: Built in the early 2000s to high standards. Excellent paint, lightly stretched upholstery. Immaculately clean and well-presented. Attractive and restrained pinstriping by Alan Johnson.

Bottom line: This is a bargain, a quality build bought for less than the sum of its parts and outside work. Sure, hot rods are individual statements of their builders, but this is classic design. Its Ford drivetrain is unusual in the genre. And if it’s not quite to the new owner’s taste and style, at this price it can be easily modified and customized to suit without affecting the concept.  

Lot 102: 1939 Peugeot 202 Berline Luxe

Sold for $17,920

Chassis no. 835646. Maroon over tan cloth. Visually maintained, largely original, #3- condition.

Equipment: 1133-cc/30-hp four-cylinder, three-speed, rear fender skirts, rear-mounted spare, red spoke wheels, Michelin X tires.

Condition: From The Maine Motorland Collection. Orange peel paint, cracks, quarter-size scrape on the left rear fender. Good upholstery. Cracked and disintegrating dash knobs. Unrestored chassis. Appears sound and usable but in cosmetically redone museum-display condition.

Bottom line: Sold at Gooding’s auction of the Merle and Peter Mullin Collection (hence the car’s museum condition) in 2024 for a huge, even grandiose, price of $42,560 and is in unchanged condition here. This result makes sense for a car with limited interest or familiarity in the U.S. and in imperfect condition.  

Lot 116: 1914 Stutz 4E Bearcat Roadster

Sold for $1,875,000

Chassis no. 2250; Engine no. AI779. Light yellow with black accents over black leather. Older restoration, #3- condition.

Equipment: RHD. 389-cid/60-hp Wisconsin T-head four-cylinder, three-speed transaxle, Warner speedometer, Phinney Walker clock, Klaxonet horn cylinder bolster tank, dual rear-mounted spares, luggage box, electric lighting.

Condition: Known for years from Thomas Powel in Middletown, RI, through Smith Hempstone Oliver, Winthrop Rockefeller’s Petit Jean Museum, Bill Harrah, James Conant, and Richard Losee, a rare continuous ownership history for over a century. An older restoration with dulling paint and worn upholstery with some seam pulls, but with impeccable provenance. Road-grimy chassis. Ideal to use and enjoy.

Bottom line: Sold by Gooding at Pebble Beach in 2006 for $715,000, then again 15 years later in 2021 for $2,920,000. It is now in somewhat more aged but still complete and drivable condition. The worm has turned on these old cars as this result indicates, dropping a notable million dollars in five years. “Appreciation” in this case will not be financial but comes from driving this monster and from sharing a place in its unbroken history, an automobile that many who know nothing of what it is or what it did recognize instantly by its name as an important, fast, rare automobile, one of America’s first sports cars. It was also, deservedly, the most expensive car at this sale.
